course.name: Model Adaptation: Fine-Tuning, Distillation and Small Models

los.description: Analyse the failures of a prompted model and assign each failure class to prompting, retrieval, tuning or distillation, given 100 bilingual requests run through the small model and a larger reference model

Prepare a tuning dataset from traces, corrections and teacher outputs, with template rendering, verifier filtering, deduplication, decontamination and personal-data removal, given 500 synthetic traces, staff corrections and a teacher model
Configure and train low-rank adapters on a 16-bit and a 4-bit base model within the memory of one free-tier GPU, given a small open-weight model and the tuning set

Evaluate the adapted model against the base and a larger prompted model with paired statistics, language slices, regression and safety checks, given a held-out bilingual test set and a general-ability check
Deploy a quantised small model with several adapters and measure throughput, latency and cost per thousand requests, given one accelerator and a target request rate
Decide whether to ship the adapted model, weighing quality, cost, licence terms and data placement, given the evaluation and load-test results

questions.prompt: Qayd writes valid calls, but for "building materials" it answers with activity code G-46. The larger model, with the same instructions, makes the same mistake. What do you try first?
options: Tune the small model on examples that contain the codes
Replace the small model with a larger one
Put the chamber's code table in the context
Add a stricter output schema
questions.explanation: Both models fail, so capability is not the cause. The table is a fact the models were never given, and it changes: it belongs in the context.
misconceptions: Treats a missing fact as a missing skill: no example set makes the model know a table that changes every year
Assumes capability is the problem, although the larger model fails in the same way
Fixes the form of an answer whose form is already valid: the schema cannot supply the right code

questions.prompt: A colleague reports: "Our adapter scores 84 on the 100 requests; the prompted model scored 27." The 27 is version 0. What does the report show?
options: Less than it claims: the adapter must be compared with the frozen baseline, 67
That tuning gained 57 points
Nothing, because 100 requests are too few to measure anything
That the adapter should be compared with the larger model only
questions.explanation: The baseline is the best prompt on the same model. Against 67 the gain is 17 points, still to be tested as a paired difference on the test set.
misconceptions: Takes the largest available difference as the effect of tuning, although 40 of those points came from words
Rejects a valid measurement for the wrong reason: 100 requests give a wide interval, but the comparison is what is wrong
Confuses the instrument with the product: the larger model is not a deployable option for the chamber

questions.prompt: A model's licence allows commercial use only to organisations with annual revenue under USD 10 million. The chamber's revenue is above that, and its registration service charges fees. What goes in the "deploy" column?
options: Yes: the weights are open, so use is free
Yes: a chamber is a non-profit body, so the limit cannot apply
Yes, once the model is fine-tuned, because the adapter is ours
Ask: counsel must decide whether a fee-charging service is commercial use
questions.explanation: The clause depends on a fact (above the threshold) and on a judgement (is the use commercial?). The engineer records both; counsel answers.
misconceptions: Reads the download as the permission: the weights are public, the right to use them commercially is conditional
Assumes a non-profit body can never make commercial use, which the licence's own definition does not say
Moves the problem instead of answering it: tuning makes a derivative work under the same licence

questions.prompt: The chamber's requests double to 80,000 a month. The accelerator still has spare capacity. What happens to the cost per thousand requests?
options: Both options stay the same
Hosted stays the same; the owned accelerator's halves
Hosted halves; the owned accelerator's stays the same
Both double
questions.explanation: A per-token price does not depend on volume. A fixed monthly cost divided by twice the requests is half the cost per request.
misconceptions: Applies the shape of a per-token price to a machine whose cost is fixed
Assumes a volume discount that a published per-token price does not contain
Treats a fixed monthly cost as if it grew with use

questions.prompt: With the frozen instructions, Qayd still takes a partner company's registration number in some requests. The code table and the schema are in the prompt. Which examples must today's tuning set contain?
options: More rows of the activity code table
Requests with two registration numbers, labelled with the applicant's own
More requests that Qayd already answers correctly
Examples of well-formed JSON
questions.explanation: A behaviour failure is fixed by examples of the right decision in the situation where the model decides wrongly. Data for tuning is chosen by failure class.
misconceptions: Adds knowledge the prompt already holds: the failure is a decision, not a missing fact
Repeats what the model already does right, which teaches the format again and the decision never
Fixes the form of a call whose form is already valid

questions.prompt: A corrected trace has the desk's call {"name": "update_record", "arguments": {"cr_number": "4031582699", "field": "city", "value": "الدمام"}}. The interface lists cities in English. What do you do with it?
options: Keep it: a human correction is always right
Change the value to "Dammam" and keep it as a correction
Drop it and count it, or send it back to the desk
Replace it with Qayd's original output
questions.explanation: The registry would reject the call, so it is not a usable label. Whatever you do with it must be visible in the counts.
misconceptions: Trusts a person's label over the tool it must call: the model would learn a value the registry refuses
Puts your own guess into the set under the desk's name, with no record of the change
Uses the model's wrong answer as a training target

questions.prompt: A teacher labelled 1,000 requests. Schema and rule checks kept 960. Nobody has read any of them. What can you state about the 960?
options: They are 96% accurate
They contain no errors, because the bad ones were rejected
They cannot be used until every one is read by staff
They are valid and consistent with their requests; their error rate is unknown until a sample is audited
questions.explanation: A verifier removes what it can detect. The rate of what it cannot detect is measured by people, on a sample, with an interval.
misconceptions: Reads yield as accuracy: passing the checks says the labels are well-formed and consistent, not right
Assumes the checks see every error, although a valid, consistent call can be the wrong decision
Discards labels that are mostly right for lack of a measurement that an audit can supply

questions.prompt: A freshly tuned adapter produces the correct tool call and then continues with more calls and stray text until the token limit. The base model never did this. Where do you look first?
options: The rendered training text: is there an end-of-turn token after the assistant's answer?
The learning rate: it was too high
The server: raise the stop-token limit
The tuning set: it needs more examples
questions.explanation: A model stops because it was shown stopping. If the training text never ends the turn, no setting teaches it to.
misconceptions: Treats a formatting fault as an optimisation problem: a lower rate would learn the same wrong text more slowly
Hides the symptom at serving time and pays for the extra tokens on every request
Blames quantity for a fault that every example shares

questions.prompt: Your overlap check flags a tuning row: "We want to renew for two years. Thank you." The same sentence is in the test set. Neither names a company or a number. What goes in the report?
options: A leak: remove it, and remove every row like it
A template collision: keep it, and report how many there are
Nothing: generic sentences need no mention
Remove the sentence from the test set instead
questions.explanation: The row carries no member's content and is how members really write. It stays, and the count goes in the report so that the reader can judge the test.
misconceptions: Treats any shared text as a leak and would delete every short, common request from training
Hides a fact that a reader of the report needs to judge the test
Changes the test set after the fact, which breaks every comparison already made on it

questions.prompt: You are about to train on 661 examples. Which check from yesterday can no longer be made once the run has finished and the loss has fallen?
options: That the tuned model beats the base on the test set
That the validation loss fell
That the rendered text ends the turn and matches the model's template
That the adapter has the intended rank
questions.explanation: A wrong rendering trains without complaint: the loss falls on whatever text it is given. It can be checked afterwards, but by then the run has been paid for.
misconceptions: Can still be made afterwards: the test set is opened on Day 4
A property of the run, read from its log after it ends
Read from the adapter's configuration at any time

questions.prompt: A base has 24 layers. You put a rank-8 adapter on the query and value projections of each layer; each is a 1,024 × 1,024 matrix. How many parameters train?
questions.explanation: Each adapted matrix adds r × (d_in + d_out) = 8 × 2,048 = 16,384. There are 2 × 24 = 48 of them: 48 × 16,384 = 786,432.
misconceptions: Counts one matrix of one layer: 8 × (1,024 + 1,024)
Counts both matrices of a layer but forgets there are 24 layers
Counts the full matrices, which are frozen: 48 × 1,024 × 1,024

questions.prompt: An accelerator has 16 GB of memory. You want to train an adapter on a base with 7 billion parameters. What does the arithmetic say?
options: Load it in 16 bits: 13 GB of weights fit in 16 GB
Load it in 4 bits: about 3.5 GB of weights, leaving room for activations
Either: only the adapter needs memory, and it is tiny
It cannot be done on this accelerator
questions.explanation: Weights are the floor. Training needs headroom for activations, which grow with batch size and sequence length; 4 bits leaves it, 16 bits does not.
misconceptions: 13 GB of weights leave about 3 GB for activations of every token in the batch: too little for training
Confuses the adapter's size with the base's: the base must still be in memory to compute anything
Ignores quantisation: 3.5 GB of weights is well inside 16 GB

questions.prompt: On 120 validation requests: rank 8 scores 101, rank 32 scores 102, rank 64 scores 100. Each is one run. Which do you choose, and on what ground?
options: Rank 8: the three cannot be told apart, and it is the cheapest
Rank 32: it has the highest score
Rank 64: more capacity is safer
Whichever scores best on the test set
questions.explanation: Differences of one or two requests are inside the noise of a single run. Among runs that cannot be told apart, take the cheapest, and say so.
misconceptions: Reads a difference of one request in 120 as real, and pays four times the parameters for it
Assumes capacity is quality, against the scores in front of you
Uses the test set to choose, which spends it

questions.prompt: A distilled student takes the partner company's registration number in requests that name two. An audit shows the teacher does the same in about one such request in five. What do you change first?
options: Train the student for more steps
Raise the adapter's rank
Lower the sampling temperature of the student
The data: correct or remove those teacher labels, or add staff corrections for that kind of request
questions.explanation: The student learnt what it was shown. A systematic error in the labels is fixed in the labels; no training setting removes it.
misconceptions: Fits the same wrong labels more closely
Adds capacity to learn the same wrong labels
Changes how the student writes, not what it was taught to decide

questions.prompt: Yesterday you chose a rank and a learning rate. A colleague suggests checking the three best settings on the test set this morning and shipping the winner. What is wrong with that?
options: The test set is too small to compare three settings
The winner's test score would then be a score it was selected on, not an estimate for new requests
Evaluating three adapters changes their weights
It takes too long
questions.explanation: Choosing is fitting. The setting was chosen on validation requests; the test set is opened once, to report the model that was already chosen.
misconceptions: The size of the test set is not the problem: 400 requests is more than validation had
Nothing in the adapters changes by being evaluated
Speed is not the issue; the meaning of the result is

questions.prompt: On 400 held-out requests a tuned model scores 352 and a larger prompted model 360. The tuned model alone is right on 18 requests, the larger alone on 26. The paired interval for the difference is −5.3 to +1.3 points. What do you write?
options: The larger model is better by 2 points
The two models are equally good
No difference is shown on this test set; the interval runs from 5.3 points worse to 1.3 better
The test is inconclusive and should not be reported
questions.explanation: An interval that contains zero supports no ranking. It does bound how much worse the tuned model can be: the owner needs that bound.
misconceptions: Reads the two totals without the interval, which contains zero
Turns 'no difference shown' into 'no difference exists': the interval allows up to 5 points
Discards a useful bound on the difference

questions.prompt: A tuned model gains 30 points on its task. On a general check it holds its score on four tasks and falls from 40 of 40 to 12 of 40 on translation. The overall general score falls by 14%. What goes in the model card?
options: The regression by task: translation fell from 40 to 12 of 40; the other four held
"General abilities: −14%"
Only the task gain: the model is for the task
"No other abilities were affected"
questions.explanation: A reader who depends on translation needs that line. An average is true and useless here; "no other abilities" claims more than was measured.
misconceptions: Hides one collapsed ability behind an average of five
Leaves out a finding a user of the model needs, because the task score is good
Draws a conclusion the check cannot support: untested abilities are unmeasured

questions.prompt: A load test gives: 4 in flight, 20 requests/s, p95 300 ms; 16 in flight, 55 requests/s, p95 900 ms; 64 in flight, 70 requests/s, p95 3,400 ms. The service must answer 95% of requests within one second. What capacity do you plan with?
options: 70 requests a second
55 requests a second
20 requests a second
About 48 requests a second, the mean of the three
questions.explanation: Capacity is the highest throughput whose latency still meets the target: 16 in flight, 55 a second, p95 of 900 ms.
misconceptions: Takes the highest throughput and ignores that one answer in twenty then takes over three seconds
Takes the lowest latency although a higher level still meets the target
Averages levels that are separate measurements

questions.prompt: A tuned small model is 3 points below a hosted larger model (interval −6 to 0). Its licence allows the use. The requests are Restricted and may not leave the organisation. Tuning removed a refusal behaviour; a replay adapter restores it at no measured cost.
options: Use the hosted model: it is better and cheaper
Ship the tuned model as it is: 3 points is small
Ship the replay adapter, gate releases on the refusal check, state the premium paid for placement
Do not ship until it matches the larger model
questions.explanation: Placement rules the hosted model out; the regression has a measured remedy; the gap is a price the owner accepts or refuses.
misconceptions: Ignores a requirement the hosted model does not meet
Ships a known regression with a tested remedy
Stops a project whose open issue has a measured fix

questions.prompt: A prompted model answers customers politely and in the right format, but quotes a renewal fee that was correct last year. Which change addresses the cause?
options: Fine-tune it on this year's conversations
Give it the current fee table in the context
Lower the sampling temperature until the fee is stable
Distil a larger model's answers into it
questions.explanation: The fee is a fact that changes; a fact belongs in the context, where it can be updated and dated.
misconceptions: Puts a changing fact into weights, where it will be wrong again next year
Treats a wrong fact as randomness in generation
Copies the larger model's behaviour, which does not contain this year's fee either

questions.prompt: On 100 requests a small model makes 30 behaviour failures and a larger model, with the same instructions, makes 4. What does the pair of counts support?
options: Tuning or distillation can teach it to the small model
The requests are too hard for any model
The small model lacks a fact that must be retrieved each time
The grading code is wrong for the small model
questions.explanation: The larger model shows that the right behaviour exists for these requests; the gap is what tuning or distillation can aim at.
misconceptions: Ignores that the larger model handles the same requests
Confuses a wrong decision with a missing fact: a missing fact would fail on both models
Blames the instrument without evidence: both models were graded by the same code

questions.prompt: A model's answer is the correct tool call, written inside a Markdown code fence instead of the required tags, and the parser rejects it. Which failure class is it?
options: Not a failure, because the decision is right
Knowledge
Behaviour
Format
questions.explanation: The decision is right and its wrapping is wrong: a schema hint, an example or tuning on the format fixes it.
misconceptions: Forgets that the registry only accepts what parses
Sees a rejected call and assumes a missing fact
Calls every wrong answer a wrong decision, although the tool and arguments are right

questions.prompt: Which task is the best candidate for a tuned small model on one accelerator?
options: Planning a company's tax filing across several systems
Answering any question about commercial law
Extracting the same eight fields from thousands of similar forms
Reviewing rare contracts that each need a lawyer's judgement
questions.explanation: One input, one structured output that a program can check, at volume: the narrow shape a small tuned model suits.
misconceptions: Chooses multi-step work that depends on intermediate results
Chooses an open-ended knowledge task, which tuning teaches badly
Chooses rare inputs that each need judgement nobody can label at volume

questions.prompt: A team reports that fine-tuning raised accuracy from 31% to 82%. The 31% used a one-sentence prompt. What should a reviewer ask for first?
options: A comparison with a model twice the size, tuned alike
The score of the best prompt on the same model
A larger training set
The training loss curve
questions.explanation: Until the untuned model has been given a strong prompt, nobody knows how much of the gain needed training.
misconceptions: Changes the question from "did tuning help this model" to "which model is bigger"
Asks for more of the thing whose effect is not yet established
Checks that training ran, not what it should be compared with

questions.prompt: Two prompt versions score 50 and 52 right out of the same 100 requests. Which statement is supported?
options: The versions cannot be told apart on this evidence
Version two would score 52% on any hundred requests
One hundred requests prove nothing about either
Version two is better by two points
questions.explanation: A difference of two requests in 100 is far inside the sampling noise of each score.
misconceptions: Treats a sample score as a property of the model
Throws away a measurement that does bound each score to about ten points either way
Reads a difference without asking how large the noise is

questions.prompt: After the baseline was frozen, an engineer improves one sentence of the instructions and keeps quoting the old score. What is wrong?
options: The set must be changed as well
The score should be averaged with the new one, weighted by date
Nothing: one sentence cannot change a score
The old score belongs to a text no longer in use
questions.explanation: A baseline is a text, a set and a score together; when the text changes, the pairing is broken.
misconceptions: Changes the second fixed element too, losing every earlier comparison
Mixes two different systems into one number
Assumes small edits have no effect, which is exactly what scoring is for

questions.prompt: A licence allows anyone to fine-tune a model for research, and allows use in a product only under a separate agreement. A company fine-tunes it and now wants to put it in its paid service. What is its position?
options: It may: the fine-tuned model is its own work
It may: research use includes testing with paying customers
It may not: adapting was licensed, this deployment is not
It may, if it does not distribute the weights
questions.explanation: Adapting and deploying are separate permissions; the adapted model is a derivative under the same terms.
misconceptions: Believes tuning creates a new work free of the original licence
Stretches "research" to cover a paid service
Mixes up distribution with commercial use: not sharing the weights does not license the use

questions.prompt: A model card shows the licence tag "other". What is the next step before choosing the model?
options: Assume it is permissive, since the weights are public
Open the licence file, read it and record the date
Ask in a forum what "other" usually means
Train first and check the licence before deployment
questions.explanation: The tag is a label; the file is the licence, and it can change with a later release.
misconceptions: Reads availability as permission
Replaces the text with someone's opinion of it
Spends the training budget before knowing whether the result can be used

questions.prompt: A licence grants commercial use only to organisations under a revenue threshold. Which pair of facts must the licence table record for an organisation that wants to deploy?
options: Its annual revenue and whether the intended use is commercial under the licence's definition
The model's size and its benchmark scores
The size of the fine-tuning set and the number of adapters served
Its number of employees and its country
questions.explanation: The clause turns on revenue against the threshold and on the purpose of the use; both are facts about the organisation.
misconceptions: Describes the model, not the licensee
Describes the project, which the clause does not depend on
Records facts the clause does not mention

questions.prompt: An owned accelerator costs SAR 6,000 a month in total and serves 30,000 requests a month. What is the cost per thousand requests?
options: SAR 180
SAR 2
SAR 20
SAR 200
questions.explanation: 6,000 divided by 30 thousands of requests is SAR 200 per thousand.
misconceptions: Multiplies the monthly cost by the volume in tens of thousands instead of dividing
Divides by 3,000 thousands: a slip of two decimal places
Divides by 300 thousands: a slip of one decimal place

questions.prompt: A hosted model costs SAR 0.50 per thousand requests and a tuned small model on the organisation's own servers costs SAR 140. The requests are classified Restricted and must stay on the organisation's servers. What should the decision memo say?
options: The small model is the cheaper option
The hosted model is chosen, because cost decides
The small model is chosen for placement, at a stated premium
Cost cannot be compared, because the two options are different
questions.explanation: The requirement rules the hosted option out; the memo states the premium honestly and why it is paid.
misconceptions: States the opposite of the measured numbers
Ignores a requirement that the cheaper option does not meet
Avoids a comparison that the same unit makes possible

questions.prompt: A prompted request carries 600 tokens of instructions and examples and 30 tokens of request. After tuning, the instructions are no longer sent. What happens to the input cost per request on a per-token price?
options: It falls by 30 tokens
It falls to about a twentieth
It stays the same, because the output is unchanged
It doubles, because adapters add tokens
questions.explanation: Input falls from about 630 tokens to about 30: the tuned model reads only the request.
misconceptions: Subtracts the request instead of the instructions
Confuses input and output tokens
Believes an adapter adds tokens: it adds weights, not text

questions.prompt: A tuning set is built only from traces that staff accepted without change. What is the model most likely to learn from it?
options: To repeat what it already does
To fix the failures staff corrected most often
To handle the hardest requests, which staff reviewed with most care
Nothing, because accepted traces carry no label
questions.explanation: An accepted trace is labelled by the model's own output, so the set repeats current behaviour.
misconceptions: Expects corrections to be present in a set that left them out
Assumes acceptance means careful review; the hardest requests are the ones staff abandoned or corrected
Forgets that the accepted output is itself the label

questions.prompt: A staff correction gives a registration number of nine digits; the tool requires ten. The intended number can be guessed from the request. What is the sound handling?
options: Use the model's original answer as the label instead
Add the missing digit and keep the row as a staff correction
Keep the row as typed, because staff labels outrank the schema
Drop the row and report it in the counts
questions.explanation: The tool would refuse the call, so it is not a usable label; dropping it visibly keeps every label traceable to its source.
misconceptions: Uses the answer that staff rejected as a training target
Enters the engineer's guess under the desk's name, with no record of the change
Trains the model to produce a call the tool refuses

questions.prompt: A verifier keeps 97% of a teacher model's labels. A colleague writes "label accuracy: 97%" in the dataset card. What is wrong with the sentence?
options: A card should not contain numbers that can change over time
Nothing: the verifier measured it
Yield counts what passed the checks, not what is right
The figure should be 3%, the share rejected
questions.explanation: Passing schema and rule checks shows a label is well-formed and consistent with its request; whether it is right needs an audit.
misconceptions: Removes the evidence a reader needs instead of correcting it
Treats passing a check as being correct
Reports the rejected share as if it were the error rate of what was kept

questions.prompt: A request names two registration numbers: the applicant's and a partner's. The teacher's call uses the partner's. Which check catches the error?
options: A rule that the number in the call must appear in the request
An audit by a person who reads the request
A check that the call parses as JSON
The schema check, because the number is invalid
questions.explanation: The call is valid and its number is in the request; only someone who makes the decision again can see that it is the wrong number.
misconceptions: Overlooks that the partner's number does appear in the request
Checks the form of a call whose form is fine
Assumes a wrong number is a malformed one: it has ten digits and passes

questions.prompt: Staff audit 30 kept teacher labels and find no error. Which statement belongs in the dataset card?
options: No error in 30, which allows a true rate up to about 11%
The audit was too small to report
The kept labels contain no errors
The error rate of the kept labels is below 1%, as the audit shows
questions.explanation: Zero in 30 bounds the rate; it does not show it is zero. The 95% upper bound is about 11%.
misconceptions: Hides a measurement that, with its bound, is useful to the reader
Reads "none found" as "none exist"
States a precision that a sample of 30 cannot give

questions.prompt: After tuning, a model writes the correct tool call and then continues generating until the token limit. The training loss fell normally. What is the most likely cause?
options: The learning rate was too low
The adapter rank was too small to learn where an answer stops
The tuning set held too few examples
The training text had no end-of-turn token after the answer
questions.explanation: A model stops because it was shown stopping; if the rendered text never closes the turn, no setting teaches it to.
misconceptions: Looks for an optimisation fault although the loss behaved normally
Treats a missing token in the data as a capacity limit
Blames quantity for a fault every example shares

questions.prompt: In a tuning example the user's request is 26 tokens and the assistant's answer 56. With a correct label mask, on how many tokens is the loss taken?
questions.explanation: The prompt is masked with the ignore index; the loss is taken on the assistant's turn only.
misconceptions: Subtracts the two counts instead of masking one of them
Supervises the request and ignores the answer: the mask reversed
Takes the loss on the whole conversation, which trains the model to predict requests

questions.prompt: A team renders its tuning set with a hand-written format and serves the adapter behind a server that applies the base model's chat template. What should they expect?
options: No effect, because the words of each example are the same
Lower quality in service than in their own evaluation
Slower training only
An error when the adapter loads
questions.explanation: The adapter learnt one string format and is sent another; their own evaluation used the hand-written format and hides the gap.
misconceptions: Ignores that role markers and special tokens are part of what the model reads
Expects a cost in speed where the cost is in what was learnt
Expects a loud failure: a format mismatch raises no error

questions.prompt: A tuning row nearly copies a test request and names the same company registration number. How is it handled?
options: Removed from the tuning set and counted as a leak
Kept, and the test request is deleted instead
Kept, because the label may differ
Kept, because near-copies are not exact copies
questions.explanation: It is a test case inside the training data: every later score would be too high by an unknown amount.
misconceptions: Changes the test set after results exist, which breaks earlier comparisons
Looks at the label although the leak is in the request the model is examined on
Applies an exact-match standard that a greeting defeats

questions.prompt: A near-duplicate rule at a lower threshold removes 82 rows; at a higher one, 67. What should decide between them?
options: The threshold used in a published paper
The lower threshold, because a smaller set trains faster
The higher threshold, because more data is always better
Reading a sample of the pairs each one removes
questions.explanation: A threshold is right when what it removes are duplicates; only reading the removed pairs shows whether different requests were merged.
misconceptions: Borrows a number tuned on other data, with other text lengths
Chooses by training time, not by whether the removed rows were duplicates
Keeps rows without asking whether they are repeats

questions.prompt: After masking, a scan for phone numbers, identity numbers, e-mail addresses and names from the member registry finds nothing. Which claim can the dataset card make?
options: The set may be published
The set contains no personal data
The scan found none of four kinds, with names taken from one list
Personal data was removed in line with the law, so no further review is needed
questions.explanation: A scan reports on what it looks for: a name outside the list, or a kind it does not know, passes.
misconceptions: Draws a release decision from a scan that covers four kinds
Turns "none found by this scan" into "none exists"
Turns one technical step into a legal conclusion

questions.prompt: Personal data is masked in the tuning set with placeholders such as [PHONE]. In service, requests reach the model unmasked. What is the main consequence?
options: None: the model ignores digits
Inputs unlike the training data, and personal data in the logs
Training must be repeated with a larger rank to absorb the digits
The adapter no longer loads on the base model
questions.explanation: The same masking function must run in front of the model in service, so that training and service inputs match.
misconceptions: Assumes a tuned model is indifferent to tokens it never saw in that position
Answers a data mismatch with a capacity setting
Expects a loading error from a difference in input text

questions.prompt: A rank-4 adapter is added to one weight matrix of shape 2,048 × 2,048. How many parameters does it add?
misconceptions: Uses rank 8, or counts the pair twice
Counts the full matrix, which stays frozen
Counts only one of the two small matrices: 4 × 2,048

questions.prompt: Before the first training step, a model with a freshly added low-rank adapter gives exactly the outputs of its base. Why?
options: The learning rate is zero during warm-up
The base model ignores adapters at inference
The adapter is switched off until the first optimiser step runs
One adapter matrix starts at zero, so the product is zero
questions.explanation: B starts at zero, so B·A adds nothing until training moves B.
misconceptions: Confuses the size of the first steps with the starting value of the weights
Contradicts what an adapter is for
Invents a switch: the adapter is active from the start and contributes zero

questions.prompt: During a run the training loss falls from 0.9 to 0.05 while the validation loss falls to 0.30 at step 150 and rises to 0.45 by step 400. What is happening, and what do you do first?
options: Normal behaviour: continue to step 800
Underfitting: raise the rank
Memorising the tuning set: stop near step 150 and check the set for near-copies
A wrong label mask: train on the whole conversation
questions.explanation: Training loss falling while validation loss rises is the signature of memorising; the cheapest fix is to stop earlier.
misconceptions: Pays for more steps of a run that is getting worse on unseen examples
Adds capacity to a run that already fits its data too closely
Proposes a rendering change that would spend the loss on the request

questions.prompt: Two adapters reach validation losses of 0.21 and 0.24. A colleague wants to ship the first on that evidence. What is missing?
options: Nothing: the lower loss is the better model, by definition of loss
The score on validation requests, graded as the tool grades
A third adapter to break the tie
The training loss of both
questions.explanation: The registry accepts a call or not; a small loss difference can go with either order of exact-match scores.
misconceptions: Treats average token likelihood as the task metric
Adds runs before measuring the two that exist
Looks at the examples the adapters were fitted to

questions.prompt: A teammate hands you an adapter file and its validation score. Which missing item most prevents you from reproducing the run?
options: The run log: base and precision, data, settings, seed and curves
The size of the adapter file in megabytes
A screenshot of the loss curve
The name of the engineer
questions.explanation: Reproducing a run needs what it was run on and with; that is what the log records.
misconceptions: Can be read from the file itself
Shows a shape but none of the settings or the data
Names who, not what was run

questions.prompt: A base model has 3 billion parameters. Roughly how much memory do its weights take at 16 bits each?
options: About 11 GB
About 48 GB
About 1.4 GB
About 5.6 GB
questions.explanation: 3 billion × 2 bytes = 6 billion bytes, about 5.6 GB.
misconceptions: Uses four bytes per weight: the 32-bit figure
Multiplies by 16 bytes instead of 16 bits
Uses half a byte per weight: the 4-bit figure

questions.prompt: A 4-bit base loads in 4 GB on a 16 GB accelerator, and training an adapter still runs out of memory. Which change addresses the cause most directly?
options: Load the base in 16 bits
Lower the adapter rank from 8 to 4, halving its parameters
Lower the batch size or the maximum sequence length
Lower the learning rate
questions.explanation: Activations grow with batch size × sequence length and are the large term above the weights.
misconceptions: Raises the floor by a factor of about four
Shrinks the smallest term: the adapter is a few megabytes
Changes the step size, not the memory

questions.prompt: An adapter was trained on a 4-bit base. Operations wants to serve it on the same base in 16 bits "for better quality". What do you advise?
options: Agree: higher precision can only help
Measure first: the adapter was fitted to the rounded weights
Refuse: an adapter cannot be loaded on a base of another precision
Agree, after doubling the adapter rank
questions.explanation: The adapter compensates partly for rounding; on unrounded weights its effect is untested until measured.
misconceptions: Assumes the adapter is independent of the weights it was trained against
States a technical impossibility that does not exist: it loads, and may behave differently
Changes the adapter without retraining it

questions.prompt: In a sweep with one run per cell, rank 4 scores 96 of 120 and rank 16 scores 97. Which conclusion is sound?
options: The two cannot be told apart; prefer rank 4
Rank 4 is better because it is smaller
The sweep must be discarded
Rank 16 is better, because it scored one request more
questions.explanation: One request in 120 is inside the noise of a single run; among equals, the cheaper setting.
misconceptions: Claims the smaller one is better in quality, which the scores do not show either
Throws away evidence that does rule out large differences
Reads one request as a real difference

questions.prompt: A team tried twelve settings and reports the test score of the one that did best on the test set. What is wrong with the reported score?
options: It is biased downward: more settings mean more noise in each score
Twelve settings are too few for any claim
Nothing, as long as the test set is large
It is biased upward: the setting was selected on the test data
questions.explanation: The best of twelve on a set is partly the luckiest of twelve on that set.
misconceptions: Gets the direction wrong: picking the maximum inflates
Blames the number of settings, not the use of the test set
Believes size removes selection bias

questions.prompt: A first adapter run shows a training loss that barely moves in 300 steps. Which setting do you examine first?
options: The rank
The adapter dropout
The learning rate
The random seed
questions.explanation: A loss that does not move is first a question of step size (after checking that anything is trainable).
misconceptions: Adds capacity when the existing capacity is not being used
Starts with a regulariser when nothing is being learnt
Expects a different seed to change whether learning happens at all

questions.prompt: In this course, a student is distilled by training it on a larger model's verified tool calls. What does the student receive from the teacher?
options: The teacher's weights, compressed
The teacher's final outputs, used as labels
The teacher's system prompt
The teacher's tokeniser
questions.explanation: Only outputs cross over: they become the labels of an ordinary tuning set.
misconceptions: Confuses distillation with compressing or copying a model
Confuses what the teacher was given with what the student learns from
Assumes shared vocabulary, which training on output text does not need

questions.prompt: A teacher labels 1 request in 50 wrongly, scattered over all kinds of request. A second teacher is wrong on every request of one rare kind and right elsewhere, also 1 in 50 overall. Which is the greater risk for the student?
options: The second: a consistent error on one kind is learnt as the rule for that kind
Neither: both are 2% noise
Both equally, because the rate is the same
The first: random errors are harder to find
questions.explanation: Scattered errors are outvoted by consistent right labels; a systematic error has nothing voting against it.
misconceptions: Treats structure in the errors as irrelevant
Reads the overall rate and ignores where the errors sit
Judges by how hard the errors are to find, not by what is learnt

questions.prompt: Which fact, on its own, rules out distilling from a hosted larger model for a government service?
options: The larger model is slower than the student
The student uses a different tokeniser
The larger model costs money for each request, and budgets are fixed
The requests are classified Restricted and may not be sent to it
questions.explanation: If the data may not reach the teacher, the teacher cannot label it; cost, speed and tokenisers are workable.
misconceptions: Applies a serving concern to a one-off labelling job
Assumes output text cannot cross between tokenisers
Treats a price as a prohibition

questions.prompt: Systems A and B score 300 and 290 on the same 400 requests. Which additional fact decides whether A is better?
options: The score of a third system
The average length of their answers, in tokens, on those requests
How many requests each gets right that the other gets wrong
The date each was evaluated
questions.explanation: 10 against 0 is a clear difference; 60 against 50 is not. The disagreements carry the evidence.
misconceptions: Adds a system instead of reading the two in hand
Looks at a property unrelated to correctness
Looks at when, not at what was measured

questions.prompt: A paired bootstrap on 400 requests resamples what, in each draw?
options: The outputs of each system separately, a thousand times each
The requests, keeping both systems' results on each one together
The tokens of each output
The two systems
questions.explanation: The request is the sampled unit; keeping the pair together is what makes the comparison paired.
misconceptions: Breaks the pairing and widens the interval
Resamples below the unit that was graded
Resamples the things being compared, of which there are two

questions.prompt: The paired interval for "tuned minus base" is +52 to +61 points; for "tuned minus larger" it is −9 to −2 points. Which summary is supported?
options: Tuning worked; the larger model is still better here
Tuning failed
Nothing can be concluded
Tuning worked, and the tuned model matches the larger one
questions.explanation: The first interval is above zero, the second below: two different sentences.
misconceptions: Ignores an interval that lies far above zero
Declines to read two intervals that both exclude zero
Ignores an interval that lies wholly below zero

questions.prompt: A tuned model is 4 points better than its alternative overall. In Arabic it is 3 points worse; in English 11 better. The service is used mostly in Arabic. What does the report lead with?
options: The English result, because it is the largest
The average of the two slices
The overall gain
The Arabic result, with its interval
questions.explanation: Report for the group the service serves; an overall figure hides the slice that matters most here.
misconceptions: Leads with the most flattering number
Replaces two findings with a figure that describes neither
Leads with an average that most users will not experience

questions.prompt: "The base is frozen, so an adapter cannot make the model forget anything." What is wrong with this statement?
options: Forgetting only happens above rank 64
Nothing: frozen weights cannot change
The base weights are intact; base plus adapter behaves differently
Adapters do change the base weights slightly, during each backward pass
questions.explanation: The adapter is added to shared matrices; the combined model can lose behaviours while the base alone still has them.
misconceptions: Invents a threshold; any rank changes behaviour
Confuses the weights with the behaviour of the adapted model
Misdescribes the method: the base is not updated

questions.prompt: A tuning set of 600 examples maps every request to a tool call. After tuning, the model answers a request for a customer's phone number with a tool call instead of declining. What is the most direct cause?
options: The learning rate was too high
The set never showed a refusal, so "always call a tool" is what it taught
The base model never refused
The test set leaked into training
questions.explanation: The adapter learnt the one rule its data was consistent with.
misconceptions: Blames a setting for a gap in the data
Contradicts the premise: the regression is a change from the base
Names a different fault, which would inflate scores, not remove refusals

questions.prompt: Which examples are suitable replay data for keeping a base model's refusal behaviour through tuning?
options: Refusal examples outside the check, mixed into the tuning set
More task examples
Examples from the test set
The items of the refusal check itself, since they are already written
questions.explanation: Replay shows the behaviour during training; the check must stay unseen to remain a check.
misconceptions: Adds more of what caused the regression
Spends the test set
Trains on the check, which then measures nothing

questions.prompt: When should the rule "which regression blocks a release" be written?
options: Only if a regression is found
By the vendor of the base model
After the tuned model's numbers are known, to fit them
Before the numbers are known
questions.explanation: A threshold chosen after seeing the result is a description of the result, not a rule.
misconceptions: Leaves no rule for the case that most needs one
Hands an owner's decision to a party who does not carry the risk
Lets the result set its own pass mark

questions.prompt: A general check of five tasks shows no regression after tuning. Which statement may the model card make?
options: "General abilities improved"
"Tuning did not affect any of the other abilities"
"No regression on the five tasks checked"
"The model is safe"
questions.explanation: A check covers what it tests; abilities outside it are unmeasured.
misconceptions: Reports a direction the check did not show
Extends five tasks to everything
Draws a safety claim from an ability check

questions.prompt: An organisation serves three tuned tasks. Each could be a fully fine-tuned copy of a 7-billion-parameter model, or one adapter on a shared base. What is the main saving of the adapter arrangement at serving time?
options: Each request needs fewer tokens
One base in memory instead of three
Adapters need no accelerator
Adapters remove the need for evaluation
questions.explanation: The base is loaded once; each task adds megabytes, not gigabytes.
misconceptions: Confuses weights with text: adapters do not shorten requests
The base still runs on the accelerator
Each adapter is a model to be evaluated

questions.prompt: In a load test, throughput rises from 20 to 55 requests a second as requests in flight go from 4 to 16. What explains the rise?
options: Requests that arrive together share each forward pass
The adapters are cached after first use, so later requests skip them
Latency falls as load rises
The model gets faster as it warms up
questions.explanation: Batching: one pass serves several requests in little more time than one.
misconceptions: Describes loading, which happens once, not per request
States the opposite of what happens: latency rises with load
Attributes a batching effect to warm-up

questions.prompt: A service answers 50,000 requests a month with a p99 latency of 4 seconds. About how many requests take longer than 4 seconds?
questions.explanation: One in a hundred of 50,000 is 500.
misconceptions: Takes one in twenty: the p95 share
Takes one in ten
Takes one in a thousand

questions.prompt: A report states: "The server handles 70 requests per second." Which addition makes the figure usable for planning?
options: The date of the test
The brand of the accelerator
The latency percentile and target at that throughput, and the failure rate
The number of adapters loaded
questions.explanation: Capacity is throughput under a latency target with no failures; without those the figure is not a capacity.
misconceptions: Adds context that does not qualify the number
Names the hardware but not what was achieved on it
Describes the configuration, not the service level

questions.prompt: A machine costs SAR 9,000 a month and can answer 2 million requests a month at its latency target. The service receives 60,000. What is the cost per thousand requests?
options: SAR 4.50
SAR 150
SAR 15
SAR 0.15
questions.explanation: 9,000 ÷ 60 thousands of requests answered = SAR 150.
misconceptions: Divides by the capacity of 2,000 thousands instead of the requests answered
Divides by 600 thousands: a slip of one decimal place
Divides by 60,000 thousands

questions.prompt: The cost per thousand requests on an owned machine is 300 times the cost at full capacity, because the machine is mostly idle. Which response addresses the cause?
options: Serve more tasks from the same base with additional adapters
Lower the adapter rank
Raise the latency target
Quantise the model further, so that each answer takes less time
questions.explanation: The cost is fixed; sharing the machine across more work is what lowers the cost of each request.
misconceptions: Shrinks a file that is not the cost
Raises a capacity that is not being used
Speeds up a machine that is already idle

questions.prompt: Which sentence belongs in the limits section of a dataset card?
options: "All personal data has been removed, as confirmed by the automatic scan"
"The dataset is unbiased"
"The dataset is of high quality"
"Accepted traces were not reviewed; an audit of 30 allows up to 11%"
questions.explanation: A limit states what was and was not checked, with numbers a reader can weigh.
misconceptions: Claims more than a scan of four kinds can support
Claims a property nobody measured
Asserts quality without evidence

questions.prompt: A decision memo recommends a tuned small model that scores below a hosted alternative and costs more per request. Which fact can still justify the recommendation?
options: Small models are the current trend
The small model was more interesting to build and the team learnt more
The data is classified so that it may not leave the organisation
The team has already spent the budget
questions.explanation: A placement requirement rules the alternative out; the memo then states the premium paid for it.
misconceptions: Appeals to fashion
Offers the team's interest as a reason for the owner
Justifies by sunk cost

questions.prompt: Evaluation shows a tuned model is worse than a hosted larger model, the data is public, and the hosted model's terms allow the use. What should the memo recommend?
options: Ship the tuned model: the work is done
Do not ship: use the hosted model, and say what would change the answer
Ship both and let users choose
Tune for another month
questions.explanation: The alternative is better and allowed; "do not ship" on good evidence is a complete answer.
misconceptions: Lets effort spent decide
Passes the decision to people without the evidence
Continues without a reason to expect a different result

questions.prompt: A model card reports the task score and the training settings. Which section is most often left out and most needed by someone deciding whether to deploy?
options: What got worse after tuning
The number of training steps
The file size of the adapter
The name of the base model
questions.explanation: Regressions are what a deployer cannot see from the task score.
misconceptions: Describes the run, not its side effects
Is a fact the file itself gives
Is usually present
